Typical_symptoms: Spindle-shaped leaf lesions with grey centres and brown margins; neck infection can cause blank panicles.
Spread_and_favourable_conditions: Wind- and rain-dispersed spores; favoured by high humidity and prolonged leaf wetness.
Diagnostic_notes: Field symptoms are suggestive; confirm by microscopy or molecular testing.

Typical_symptoms: Oval brown lesions with grey or whitish centres, often with yellow halos; spots may occur on grains.
Spread_and_favourable_conditions: Seed-borne and residue-borne; favoured by warm, humid conditions and plant stress.
Diagnostic_notes: Can be confused with other leaf-spot diseases.

Typical_symptoms: Water-soaked streaks from leaf tips or margins that turn yellow and then straw-coloured.
Spread_and_favourable_conditions: Rain splash, irrigation water and wounds; favoured by warm, wet weather.
Diagnostic_notes: Yellow bacterial ooze may be observed from fresh cut lesions.

Typical_symptoms: Oval or irregular greenish-grey lesions on leaf sheaths near the waterline, later becoming tan with darker margins.
Spread_and_favourable_conditions: Soil- and residue-borne; spreads through plant contact in dense, humid canopies.
Diagnostic_notes: Web-like fungal growth may occur under humid conditions.

Typical_symptoms: Individual grains are replaced by velvety orange to greenish smut balls.
Spread_and_favourable_conditions: Spores spread by air; infection occurs around flowering.
Diagnostic_notes: Smut balls are a characteristic field sign.

Typical_symptoms: Elongated reddish-brown pustules on stems and leaf sheaths; later pustules turn black.
Spread_and_favourable_conditions: Airborne spores; alternate host barberry is involved in some regions.
Diagnostic_notes: Pustule colour and location help distinguish rust types.

Typical_symptoms: Small orange-brown, round to oval pustules scattered mainly on leaf blades.
Spread_and_favourable_conditions: Airborne urediniospores; favoured by mild temperatures and leaf wetness.
Diagnostic_notes: Differentiate from stripe rust by pustule arrangement and colour.

Typical_symptoms: Kernels are replaced by black powdery spores; infected heads often emerge earlier than healthy heads.
Spread_and_favourable_conditions: Internally seed-borne; infection occurs at flowering and persists in embryo.
Diagnostic_notes: Black spore masses are a strong diagnostic clue.

Typical_symptoms: Long, cigar-shaped grey-green to tan lesions on leaves, often starting on lower leaves.
Spread_and_favourable_conditions: Residue-borne spores spread by wind and rain; favoured by prolonged humidity.
Diagnostic_notes: Lesion shape is characteristic but laboratory confirmation may be needed.

Typical_symptoms: Small tan lesions that enlarge into elongated, rectangular or oval necrotic spots.
Spread_and_favourable_conditions: Crop residue and airborne spores; favoured by warm, humid weather.
Diagnostic_notes: Symptoms vary with pathogen race and host genotype.

Typical_symptoms: Small, raised, reddish-brown to cinnamon pustules on both leaf surfaces.
Spread_and_favourable_conditions: Airborne spores; favoured by cool to moderate temperatures and high humidity.
Diagnostic_notes: Pustules can be rubbed off, leaving exposed tissue.

Typical_symptoms: Water-soaked, soft stalk tissues with internal decay; plants may lodge and emit an unpleasant odour.
Spread_and_favourable_conditions: Enters through wounds and spreads in wet conditions.
Diagnostic_notes: Soft rot and odour are not unique; confirm in the laboratory.

Causal_organism: Alternaria linariae (syn. Alternaria solani in older literature)
Typical_symptoms: Brown leaf spots with concentric rings, often surrounded by yellowing; lower leaves are commonly affected first.
Spread_and_favourable_conditions: Survives on crop debris and spreads by rain splash; favoured by warm, humid conditions.
Diagnostic_notes: Concentric target-like rings are a useful clue.

Typical_symptoms: Water-soaked, rapidly enlarging dark lesions; white growth may appear on leaf undersides in humid weather.
Spread_and_favourable_conditions: Wind- and rain-dispersed sporangia; favoured by cool, wet conditions.
Diagnostic_notes: Rapid progression and white sporulation support diagnosis.

Typical_symptoms: Sudden wilting while leaves may remain green; vascular browning and bacterial streaming may occur.
Spread_and_favourable_conditions: Soil- and water-borne; enters through roots and wounds.
Diagnostic_notes: A cut-stem streaming test is presumptive, not definitive.

Typical_symptoms: Upward leaf curling, yellowing, stunting and reduced fruit set.
Spread_and_favourable_conditions: Transmitted persistently by whiteflies (Bemisia tabaci).
Diagnostic_notes: Virus testing is needed to distinguish it from nutritional or other viral disorders.

Causal_organism: Streptomyces scabiei and related pathogenic Streptomyces spp.
Typical_symptoms: Raised, corky or pitted lesions on tuber surfaces.
Spread_and_favourable_conditions: Soil- and seed-tuber-associated; favoured by susceptible cultivars and suitable soil conditions.
Diagnostic_notes: Tuber symptoms can resemble other skin disorders.

Typical_symptoms: Black, soil-like sclerotia adhere to tuber skin; sprouts and stems may be affected.
Spread_and_favourable_conditions: Soil- and seed-tuber-borne.
Diagnostic_notes: Sclerotia can usually be scraped from the tuber surface.

Typical_symptoms: Water-soaked leaf lesions rapidly turn brown or black; tubers may develop firm, reddish-brown internal rot.
Spread_and_favourable_conditions: Wind- and rain-dispersed inoculum; favoured by cool, wet weather.
Diagnostic_notes: Inspect foliage and tubers; laboratory confirmation can distinguish tuber rots.

Causal_organism: Colletotrichum scovillei and related Colletotrichum spp.
Typical_symptoms: Sunken, circular fruit lesions with dark margins; salmon-coloured spore masses may develop.
Spread_and_favourable_conditions: Seed- and residue-associated; spreads by rain splash.
Diagnostic_notes: Several Colletotrichum species cause similar symptoms.

Typical_symptoms: Small water-soaked spots that become dark, angular or irregular lesions; severe infection causes defoliation.
Spread_and_favourable_conditions: Seed-borne and splash-dispersed.
Diagnostic_notes: Species-level identification requires laboratory testing.

Typical_symptoms: Leaf spots, stem lesions and fruit rot; fruits may show sunken areas with small black fruiting bodies.
Spread_and_favourable_conditions: Seed- and residue-borne; spreads in wet weather.
Diagnostic_notes: Multiple plant parts may show symptoms.

Typical_symptoms: Rapid wilting, vascular browning and possible bacterial streaming from cut stems.
Spread_and_favourable_conditions: Soil- and water-borne.
Diagnostic_notes: Confirm with validated laboratory methods.

Typical_symptoms: V-shaped yellow lesions from leaf margins with blackened veins; vascular tissues may darken.
Spread_and_favourable_conditions: Seed-borne and spread by rain splash and handling.
Diagnostic_notes: V-shaped lesions and black veins are characteristic.

Typical_symptoms: Swollen, club-shaped roots; plants become stunted and wilt during warm periods.
Spread_and_favourable_conditions: Long-lived resting spores persist in soil; spread by contaminated soil and water.
Diagnostic_notes: Root inspection is essential for diagnosis.

Disease: Tikka leaf spot (early and late leaf spots)
Typical_symptoms: Brown to black leaf spots, sometimes with yellow halos; severe infection causes premature defoliation.
Spread_and_favourable_conditions: Crop debris and airborne or splash-dispersed spores.
Diagnostic_notes: Early and late leaf spots require careful differentiation.

Typical_symptoms: Small orange-brown pustules, mainly on the lower leaf surface; leaves may dry and shed.
Spread_and_favourable_conditions: Airborne spores; favoured by humid conditions.
Diagnostic_notes: Pustules are a useful field sign.

Typical_symptoms: Internal stalk tissue shows characteristic red discoloration with intermittent white patches; canes may dry out.
Spread_and_favourable_conditions: Primarily infected setts and crop debris.
Diagnostic_notes: Split-stalk examination is useful; confirm suspected cases in the laboratory.

Typical_symptoms: A long, black whip-like structure emerges from the growing point.
Spread_and_favourable_conditions: Infected setts and airborne spores.
Diagnostic_notes: The whip-like sorus is a distinctive sign.

Causal_organism: Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cubense species complex
Typical_symptoms: Older leaves yellow and collapse; vascular tissues show reddish-brown to dark discoloration.
Spread_and_favourable_conditions: Soil-borne chlamydospores; spread by infected planting material and contaminated soil.
Diagnostic_notes: Race or lineage identification requires specialised testing.

Typical_symptoms: Narrow reddish-brown streaks develop into dark leaf lesions, reducing functional leaf area.
Spread_and_favourable_conditions: Wind- and rain-dispersed spores; favoured by humid conditions.
Diagnostic_notes: Leaf symptoms can overlap with other Sigatoka diseases.

Typical_symptoms: Dark, irregular leaf and flower lesions; fruits develop sunken black spots and may rot after harvest.
Spread_and_favourable_conditions: Rain-splashed spores; latent infections can develop during ripening.
Diagnostic_notes: Post-harvest symptoms may arise from infections acquired before harvest.

Typical_symptoms: White powdery growth on panicles, flowers and young fruits; flower and fruit drop may occur.
Spread_and_favourable_conditions: Airborne conidia; favoured by suitable mild, humid conditions.
Diagnostic_notes: White superficial growth is a key field clue.

Typical_symptoms: Raised, corky lesions with yellow halos on leaves, twigs and fruits; lesions may occur on both leaf surfaces.
Spread_and_favourable_conditions: Wind-driven rain and contaminated tools; entry through stomata and wounds.
Diagnostic_notes: Characteristic crater-like lesions; follow local quarantine guidance.

Typical_symptoms: Mosaic and distortion of leaves; oily streaks on petioles and ring-shaped markings on fruits.
Spread_and_favourable_conditions: Non-persistent transmission by aphids; also spread through infected planting material in some contexts.
Diagnostic_notes: Symptoms are suggestive; confirm with virus testing.

Typical_symptoms: Yellow oil spots on upper leaf surfaces and white downy growth beneath; berries may become infected.
Spread_and_favourable_conditions: Rain-splashed and airborne sporangia; favoured by warm, wet conditions.
Diagnostic_notes: White downy sporulation on leaf undersides is a useful clue.

Typical_symptoms: Small water-soaked lesions enlarge into purple, elliptical spots with yellow zones; leaves may blight.
Spread_and_favourable_conditions: Crop debris and airborne spores; favoured by leaf wetness.
Diagnostic_notes: Can be confused with Stemphylium leaf blight.

Typical_symptoms: Yellowing of veins and veinlets, mosaic appearance, stunting and small or malformed fruits.
Spread_and_favourable_conditions: Transmitted by whiteflies (Bemisia tabaci).
Diagnostic_notes: Virus identity should be confirmed by molecular testing.

Typical_symptoms: Small tan to reddish-brown lesions with raised pustules, often on lower leaf surfaces.
Spread_and_favourable_conditions: Airborne urediniospores; favoured by prolonged leaf wetness.
Diagnostic_notes: Microscopy or molecular testing helps distinguish rusts.

Typical_symptoms: Angular leaf spots, black lesions on veins and stems, and boll lesions in severe cases.
Spread_and_favourable_conditions: Seed-borne and splash-dispersed.
Diagnostic_notes: Symptoms vary with plant age and cultivar.

Typical_symptoms: White fungal growth around the stem base with small mustard-seed-like brown sclerotia; plants wilt.
Spread_and_favourable_conditions: Soil-borne; favoured by warm, moist soil.
Diagnostic_notes: Sclerotia and basal mycelium are useful diagnostic signs.
